lines.text: ay Period three graph has several bends and one striking jump. Understanding where each appears lets you recognise an element from a physical property clue.

Across Period three, atomic radius decreases as nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same main shell and inner shell shielding stays approximately constant. Common ionic radii decrease from sodium plus to aluminium three plus, jump to the larger anions, then decrease from phosphorus three minus to chloride, each of those groups is isoelectronic. Melting point rises from sodium through magnesium and aluminium to a maximum at silicon, falls sharply at P, rises at S, then falls at chlorine and Ar. sodium, magnesium and aluminium conduct electricity well, silicon is a semiconductor, P, S, chlorine and Ar do not conduct. The repeating variation in properties across a period is periodicity.
The radius argument extends your earlier work on nuclear charge and shielding. The irregular melting point and conductivity patterns become meaningful once you classify each element's structure.

Atomic radius decreases across Period three as nuclear attraction rises. Common cation radii decrease, a jump separates them from the larger anions, whose radii then decrease. Melting point peaks at silicon, drops at P, rises at S, then falls to Ar. sodium, magnesium and aluminium conduct well, silicon is a semiconductor, P, S, chlorine and Ar do not conduct. Before reading the explanation, predict whether the radius rises or falls from aluminium three plus to phosphorus three minus, which occupied shells would you compare?
Why can you describe the ionic radii as two decreasing series but not as one smooth decrease across the period?

Which change occurs from sodium plus to aluminium three plus? Ionic radius decreases. Ionic radius increases. A new occupied shell is added. Nuclear charge decreases. ay These ions have the same electron configuration, but nuclear charge rises.
Silicon melts far above sulfur but conducts far worse than aluminium. Structure and bonding explain both comparisons.

sodium, magnesium and aluminium have metallic lattices. From sodium to aluminium, smaller ions with greater charge attract more delocalised electrons more strongly, so melting points rise, mobile delocalised electrons carry current. silicon has a giant covalent lattice, many strong silicon silicon bonds must break on melting, giving the period's highest melting point. silicon is a semiconductor, not a good metal like conductor. P four, S eight and C L two are simple molecules, and Ar is monatomic. Melting overcomes weak instantaneous dipole induced dipole attractions between their particles, it does not break the covalent bonds inside molecules. S eight has stronger attractions than P four because it is larger and has more electrons. These non metals lack mobile charged particles, so they do not conduct.
Use the structure categories from bonding, metallic, giant covalent, simple molecular and monatomic. For every property, name the particles that move or the attraction that melting overcomes.

sodium aluminium, stronger metallic bonding raises melting points, mobile delocalised electrons conduct. silicon, giant covalent lattice, high melting point, semiconductor. P four, S eight, C L two and Ar, weak attractions between particles give lower melting points. P, S, chlorine and Ar have no mobile charged particles and do not conduct. Before reading the explanation, predict the melting point change from aluminium to silicon and the conductivity change from magnesium to silicon, which feature of bonding controls each?
What is broken when sulfur melts, and how does that differ from what is broken when silicon melts?

Why is silicon's melting point much higher than sulfur's? silicon silicon covalent bonds in a giant lattice are much stronger than attractions between S eight molecules. Silicon molecules have stronger intermolecular forces. Sulfur has weak covalent bonds within S eight that break on melting. Silicon has more delocalised electrons than sulfur. ay Silicon is giant covalent, sulfur is simple molecular, so different attractions are overcome on melting.

Elements D and E are both in Period three. Element D has the smallest atomic radius in Period three. There are only two elements in Period three which have a lower melting point than element E. Elements D and E react together to form compound L. Which compound could be L?

Chlorine has the smallest atomic radius and phosphorus has the third lowest melting point, only argon and chlorine are lower. Thus P C L three fits. M G C L two is wrong because magnesium is too high melting.

X, Y and Z are consecutive elements in Period three of the Periodic Table. Element Y has the highest first ionisation energy and the lowest melting point of these three elements. What are the identities of X, Y and Z? X. Y. Z.

Phosphorus lies between silicon and sulfur. Its simple molecular structure gives the lowest melting point of the three, while its first ionisation energy exceeds sulfur's owing to the half filled three p subshell.

Which statements are correct going across Period three from sodium to chlorine? one. The charge on the nucleus increases, pulling the electrons closer to it. two. The radius of the most common ion of each element decreases. three. The shielding caused by inner electrons decreases, so the outer electrons are pulled closer to the nucleus.

Nuclear charge increases and outer electrons occupy the same main shell, so atomic radius falls. Common ionic radii do not decrease smoothly because of the jump from small cations to larger anions, inner shell shielding does not decrease.

Which statements help to explain the increase in melting point from sodium to aluminium? one. The charge on the metal ion increases. two. There are more delocalised electrons per metal ion. three. The radius of the metal ion decreases.
All three stated changes strengthen metallic bonding, greater cation charge, more delocalised electrons and smaller ions. A first ionisation energy trend alone does not explain the melting points.

The melting points of the Period three elements sodium to aluminium are shown in the table. element. sodium. magnesium. aluminium melting point or K. three hundred and seventy one. nine hundred and twenty three. nine hundred and thirty two. Which factor explains the increase in melting points from sodium to aluminium?
More outer electrons contribute to the delocalised sea from sodium to aluminium, strengthening metallic bonding. Increasing relative atomic mass does not explain this rise.
Which row gives the best description of the variations in the melting points and the first ionisation energies of the elements in Period three from sodium to argon?

D is the best overall description, first ionisation energies generally increase across Period three, with dips at aluminium and sulfur. Melting point reaches its maximum at silicon, not aluminium, the subsequent overall decrease includes a rise from phosphorus to sulfur, so it is not monotonic.
X and Y are atoms of different elements in Period three of the Periodic Table. Neither X nor Y is argon. X is a non metal. X has a greater atomic radius than Y. Which statement is correct?
Atomic radius decreases across Period three. A non metal X with larger radius than Y must lie before Y, so Y is also a non metal, X cannot have more protons.
Which row about silicon, silicon, and magnesium, magnesium, and their ions is correct?

D is correct, silicon four plus and magnesium two plus each have ten electrons, but silicon has fourteen protons and magnesium has twelve, so the greater nuclear attraction makes silicon four plus smaller. ay has the atomic radius trend reversed. B gives a true conductivity comparison but a false explanation, silicon does not have four delocalised electrons per atom. C has the melting point comparison reversed, silicon melts at a higher temperature than magnesium.
Which statement is correct?
Magnesium conducts better than sodium because it supplies more delocalised electrons and has stronger metallic bonding. Silicon is smaller, not larger, than aluminium.

X and Y are two elements from Period three of the Periodic Table. Element X has a higher electrical conductivity than element Y. Element Y has a higher melting point than element X. Which formula is a compound formed from element X and element Y?
Magnesium conducts better than silicon, but silicon melts at a higher temperature, M G two S I is the corresponding compound. N ay C L fails the melting point ordering.

Elements Y and Z are both in Period three. Element Y has the smallest atomic radius in Period three. There are only two elements in Period three that have a lower melting point than element Z. Elements Y and Z react together to form compound R. Which compound could be R?
Y is chlorine, Z is phosphorus, whose melting point is exceeded below only by chlorine and argon. They form P C L three. Magnesium has a much higher melting point.
Which set of three elements contains a single element that has both the highest melting point and the lowest electrical conductivity of the three elements in the set?
Silicon has the highest melting point and lowest conductivity among magnesium, aluminium and silicon. In the aluminium silicon phosphorus set, phosphorus conducts least but silicon melts highest.

It decreases as nuclear charge increases within the same occupied main shell. The tempting alternative in B is wrong, It increases because an electron is added at each step.

It rises through the metals to a maximum at silicon, then falls sharply at phosphorus, rises at sulfur and falls through chlorine to argon. The tempting alternative in B is wrong, It increases steadily to argon.

The relative melting points of four consecutive elements in the Periodic Table are shown in the graph. The elements all have proton numbers less than twenty. Which element is in Group sixteen? melting point or K. two hundred and seventy three.

Which rows correctly show the relative electrical conductivities of the sets of three Period three elements? greatest conductivity least conductivity. one sodium silicon chlorine. two aluminium magnesium phosphorus. three sulfur silicon phosphorus.

Which rows correctly show the relative electrical conductivities of the sets of three Period three elements? greatest conductivity least conductivity. one sodium silicon chlorine. two aluminium magnesium phosphorus. three sulfur silicon phosphorus.

L and M are elements in Period three of the Periodic Table. The oxide of L is a solid at room temperature. This oxide has a giant structure. The chloride of L does not react with water. Argon is the only element in Period three with a lower melting point than M. Which formula represents a compound of elements L and M?
Which statement explains why calcium has a higher melting point than barium?

ay is correct. This applies the metallic bonding model used for Period three to two Group two metals, both supply two delocalised electrons per atom, but the smaller calcium cations attract the delocalised electrons more strongly. Both metals have metallic structures, additional electron shells do not explain the trend by increased repulsion.
The diagram shows the melting points of eight elements with consecutive atomic numbers. Which element could be sodium? melting point or K atomic number.

X, Y and Z are elements all found within Groups thirteen, fourteen and fifteen of the Periodic Table. X is in the same group in the Periodic Table as Y. Y and Z are in Period three. The first ionisation energy of X is greater than the first ionisation energy of Y. The melting point of Z is less than the melting point of Y. Y and Z both form chlorides which are white solids. These white solids react with water to produce solutions with a p H of less than four. Which row of the table shows the possible identities of X and Y?

ay is correct, with X equals boron, Y equals aluminium and Z equals phosphorus. The chloride clues are consistent with solid ay L C L three and P C L five. X must be above Y in its group to have the higher first ionisation energy, eliminating B and C. D is tempting, but if Y were phosphorus, neither aluminium nor silicon could be Z because both melt at higher temperatures than phosphorus, the required lower melting point is impossible.
Which statement is correct?

Which statements are correct? one. All the elements in the table with a giant structure have a higher melting point than each of the elements in the table with a simple molecular structure. two. Magnesium has a higher melting point than sodium because it has more delocalised electrons and stronger electrostatic attraction between the delocalised electrons and the metal ions. three. Phosphorus and sulfur do not conduct electricity because they are simple molecular solids at room conditions.
Explain why silicon has a much higher melting point than sulfur. Compare their structures and identify the attractions overcome during melting.

Silicon forms a giant covalent lattice, whereas sulfur consists of S eight molecules. Breaking strong silicon silicon covalent bonds requires much more energy than overcoming the weaker instantaneous dipole induced dipole attractions between sulfur molecules, S S bonds within the molecules remain intact.
Think about what particles make up each solid.
Organise your comparison as structure, attraction overcome, then energy required.
For each solid, decide whether melting separates molecules or disrupts a continuous bonded network.
At room temperature, magnesium conducts electricity much better than pure silicon. Explain this difference in terms of bonding and mobile charge carriers.

Magnesium has mobile delocalised electrons that carry charge through its metallic lattice. Silicon is giant covalent and a semiconductor, with far fewer mobile charge carriers at room temperature, so pure silicon conducts much less well.
Focus on how charge can move through a solid.
Identify the bonding in each element, then distinguish total outer electrons from mobile charge carriers.
Start by asking whether the outer electrons can move throughout each lattice or are mainly involved in bonds.

Melting point rises from sodium through magnesium and aluminium to the maximum at silicon, falls sharply to P, rises to S, then falls through chlorine to the minimum at Ar. A continuous decrease after silicon misses the P to S rise.

In one breath.

Across sodium to argon, atomic and ionic sizes, melting point and electrical conductivity change in recognisable patterns. Explain each pattern using nuclear attraction, structure and bonding rather than memorising a single rising or falling line.
Key ideas.

Atomic radius. From sodium towards chlorine, atomic radius decreases. Proton number and nuclear charge increase, while added electrons enter the same main shell and shielding by inner shells stays approximately constant. Stronger attraction draws the outer shell closer. Argon is often omitted from comparisons of covalent atomic radii because it does not normally form covalent bonds.

Ionic radius. Do not draw one smooth trend through every common ion. sodium plus, magnesium two plus and aluminium three plus are isoelectronic, increasing nuclear charge makes their radii decrease. There is a large jump to the anions phosphorus three minus, sulfide and chloride, whose electrons occupy the third shell. These three ions are also isoelectronic, their radii decrease as nuclear charge increases. The common ion of silicon is not normally included in this simple comparison.
Two separate decreasing series, the cations have two occupied shells, while the anions have three. The gap is a jump to larger ions, not a connecting trend through silicon, heights are schematic.

Melting point. Sodium, magnesium and aluminium are metals. Their melting points rise because the metallic bonds strengthen, cation charge increases, cation radius decreases and the number of delocalised electrons per atom increases. Silicon has the highest melting point, it is a giant covalent lattice with many strong silicon silicon bonds to break. Phosphorus exists as P four molecules, sulfur as S eight molecules and chlorine as C L two molecules. Melting these substances overcomes weak instantaneous dipole induced dipole attractions between molecules, not the covalent bonds within them. Sulfur melts above phosphorus because larger S eight molecules have more electrons and stronger intermolecular attractions. Chlorine melts lower, monatomic argon has the lowest melting point.

sodium aluminium, strengthening metallic bonding, silicon, the giant covalent peak, P S chlorine, simple molecular substances, with stronger attractions between S eight molecules than between P four molecules, Ar, monatomic, with very weak attractions between atoms. Heights show the qualitative pattern, not a numerical scale.

Electrical conductivity. sodium, magnesium and aluminium conduct well because mobile delocalised electrons carry charge through their metallic lattices. Aluminium generally conducts best of the three. Silicon is a semiconductor, its conductivity is far below that of the metals, although it can increase with temperature. P, S, chlorine and Ar lack mobile charged particles and do not conduct electricity in their elemental forms.
Method.
Place the elements in Period three order, sodium, magnesium, aluminium, silicon, P, S, chlorine, Ar.
For a radius comparison, check whether the particles are atoms, cations or anions. Compare isoelectronic ions within their own series.
For melting or conductivity, identify the structure first, metallic, giant covalent, simple molecular or monatomic.
Name the attraction overcome on melting, or the mobile charge carrier for conductivity. Link its strength or availability to the observed property.
Worked example.

Explain why silicon has a much higher melting point than sulfur. Silicon has a giant covalent lattice. Melting it requires many strong silicon silicon covalent bonds to be broken. Sulfur consists of S eight molecules. Melting sulfur overcomes much weaker instantaneous dipole induced dipole attractions between molecules, the S S bonds within each molecule remain intact.
Traps.

Trap, Ionic radius decreases smoothly from sodium plus to chloride. Why it's wrong, The cations lose the third shell, while the anions retain it. Instead, Describe the two decreasing isoelectronic series and the jump between them.
Trap, Silicon has strong intermolecular forces. Why it's wrong, Its atoms form one giant covalent network. Instead, Name the silicon silicon covalent bonds that must be broken.

Trap, Silicon conducts like aluminium because it has four outer electrons. Why it's wrong, Those electrons participate in covalent bonds. Instead, Contrast a semiconductor with mobile delocalised electrons in a metal.
Exam technique.

For describe, give the pattern including its peak, jump or reversal. For explain, give the structure, the relevant particles or bonds, and the causal link to the property. When comparing silicon and sulfur, identify exactly which attractions are overcome on melting.
